## Goal

Demonstrate the central limit theorem

### Subgoals

- Learn about RMarkdown (the thing you're reading now)
- Refactor some code, think about simplification

### prerequisites for the central limit demonstration

- generator of numbers from some distribution
- give some impression of the distribution
- display the distribution of the means

Let's have a look at how to create some skewed distributions with built-in R functions

```{r distributions}

# The following example was taken from: https://statisticsglobe.com/draw-normal-left-right-skewed-distributions-r

set.seed(35486)                    # Create random distributions
data <- data.frame(x1 = rbeta(1000, 10, 2),
                   x2 = rbeta(1000, 5, 2),
                   x3 = rnorm(1000),
                   x4 = rbeta(1000, 2, 5),
                   x5 = rbeta(1000, 2, 10))

head(data)                         # Print head of data
```
As you can see, we're using the beta distribution, which is defined as

$\mathrm{Beta}(\alpha, \beta) = \displaystyle \frac{x^{\alpha-1}(1-x)^{\beta-1}}{B(\alpha,\beta)}$

where

$\mathrm{B}(\alpha, \beta)=\displaystyle \frac{\Gamma(\alpha)\Gamma(\beta)}{\Gamma(\alpha + \beta)}$

and $\Gamma$ is the Gamma function: $\Gamma(z) = \displaystyle \int_{0}^{\infty} t^{z-1} e^{-t}\mathrm dt$

see also https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beta_distribution

All of this is not very relevant here, but to show how to write maths: https://rpruim.github.io/s341/S19/from-class/MathinRmd.html

## Here are some plots to show what the distributions look like graphically

Here I've used 'base R' functions, because we're going to talk about ggplot2 later in this course.

```{r densityplots, echo=FALSE}
plot(density(data$x1), col = 2,    # Overlay all columns as densities
     xlim = c(- 3, 3),
     ylim = c(0, 5))
lines(density(data$x2), col = 3)

lines(density(data$x3), col = 4)
lines(density(data$x4), col = 5)
lines(density(data$x5), col = 6)
legend("topleft",                  # Add legend to plot
       legend = c("x1 = rbeta(1000, 10, 2)",
                  "x2 = rbeta(1000, 5, 2)",
                  "x3 = rnorm(1000)",
                  "x4 = rbeta(1000, 2, 5)",
                  "x5 = rbeta(1000, 2, 10)"),
       col = 2:6,
       lty = 1,
       cex = 0.8)

```

Note that the `echo = FALSE` parameter was added to the code chunk to prevent printing of the R code that generated the plot.

# Assignment

## Laying the basis: Initial functions

- Create a function to create a list with 300 vectors with 1000 samples each using one of the rbeta distributions (pick your own parameters)
- Create a function to calculate a vector with the averages of all of these vectors
- Create q-q plots. Use this to show the normality of one of the original distributions, and of the resulting averages vector

```{r initial function}

generate_dataset <- function() {
  result <- list()
  for (i in 1:300) {
    result[[i]] <- rbeta(1000, 2, 5)
  }
  return(result)
}

calculate_mean_values <- function(dataset) {
  result <- c()
  for (i in 1:300) {
    result <- c(result, mean(dataset[[i]]))
  }
  return(result)
}

random_samples <- generate_dataset()
mean_values <- calculate_mean_values(random_samples)

qqnorm(random_samples[[1]])
qqnorm(mean_values)

```

## Refactoring: adding functionality

We'd like to be able to set the number of datasets, and the number of samples per dataset. Copy the code block from above (not very DRY, but you will have the history of your thought process in this document)

the generate_dataset function should now take some arguments, being n for the number of datasets, and m for the number of samples in each dataset

We're *refactoring*, so make sure that the **generate_dataset()** call still works.

```{r first parameters}

generate_dataset <- function(n = 300, m = 1000) {
  result <- list()
  for (i in 1:n) {
    result[[i]] <- rbeta(m,2,5)
  }
  return(result)
}

calculate_mean_values <- function(dataset) {
  result <- c()
  for (i in 1:length(dataset)) {
    result <- c(result, mean(dataset[[i]]))
  }
  return(result)
}

random_samples <- generate_dataset()
mean_values <- calculate_mean_values(random_samples)

qqnorm(random_samples[[1]])
qqnorm(mean_values)

```

```{r add alpha and beta parameters}
generate_dataset <- function(n = 300, m = 1000, alpha=2, beta=5) {
  result <- list()
  for (i in 1:n) {
    result[[i]] <- rbeta(m, alpha, beta)
  }

}

calculate_mean_values <- function(dataset) {

    result <- c(result, mean(dataset[[i]]))
  }

}

random_samples_old_method <- generate_dataset() # still works
random_samples <- generate_dataset(300, 1000, 1, 3)

mean_values <- calculate_mean_values(random_samples)

qqnorm(random_samples[[1]])
qqnorm(mean_values)
```

# Demonstrating the Central Limit Theorem

The Central Limit Theorem states that the *mean of the means* of measurements with wildly different distributions, will tend to have a normal distribution.

## Random dataset generator

To demonstrate this principle, we'll create a function to calculate a large number of samples. The function can use many different types of random generation functions such as runif, rnorm or rbeta.  

The function creates a list with a selectable number of predefined vectors, each vector with a user-defined number of random samples. The function to create random numbers is also included.

```{r random generator}
generate_dataset <- function(n = 300, m = 1000, func=rbeta, ...) {
  result <- list()
  for (i in 1:n) {
    result[[i]] <- func(m, ...)
  }
  return(result)
}
```

## Means of all the vectors

The following function will calculate the mean of all the separate vectors in the list. The output is a vector with these mean values.

```{r calculate the mean}

calculate_mean_values <- function(dataset) {
  result <- c()
  for (i in 1:length(dataset)) {
    result <- c(result, mean(dataset[[i]]))
  }
  return(result)
}

```

## Executing the functions to test different distributions

As two simple examples, we'll be testing the uniform distribution (with runif) and a Beta distribution with $\alpha = 10$ and $\beta = 2$ (with rbeta)

```{r central limit example}
random_samples_beta <- generate_dataset(800, 1000, rbeta, 10, 2)
random_samples_unif <- generate_dataset(800, 1000, runif)

mean_values_beta <- calculate_mean_values(random_samples_beta)
mean_values_unif <- calculate_mean_values(random_samples_unif)
```

### Uniform and beta distributions

```{r show distributions of runif and rbeta}

plot(density(random_samples_beta[[1]]), main="rbeta(10,2) vs runif")
lines(density(random_samples_unif[[1]]), col="red")
```

Clearly these distributions are very different and both are not normally distributed. Now if we look at the means, we *do* see a normal distribution.

```{r show distribution of the means}

plot(density(mean_values_beta), main="means of rbeta(10,2)")
plot(density(mean_values_unif), col="red", main="means of runif")

```

Of course the mean values are different, but their *distribution* follows the normal distribution, as can be show with q-q plots:
 
```{r qqplots}
 
qqnorm(mean_values_beta, main="beta distribution means")
qqline(mean_values_beta)

qqnorm(mean_values_unif, main="uniform distribution means")
qqline(mean_values_unif)
```

To show that these are limits for basically infinite numbers of samples, let's have a look at much lower numbers.

```{r low numbers }
random_samples_beta2 <- generate_dataset(20, 20, rbeta, 10, 2)
random_samples_unif2 <- generate_dataset(20, 20, runif)

mean_values_beta2 <- calculate_mean_values(random_samples_beta2)
mean_values_unif2 <- calculate_mean_values(random_samples_unif2)

qqnorm(mean_values_beta2, main="beta distribution means")
qqline(mean_values_beta2)

qqnorm(mean_values_unif2, main="uniform distribution means")
qqline(mean_values_unif2)

```

# Addressing some code smells

Doing it in a complicated way :)

If you want to demonstrate that means calculated from different distributions all end up in a normal distribution, it's nice to be able to automate it in a loop.  
Here I demonstrate how this can be done, unfortunately it's a bit more complex code, because some of the distributions need arguments for their '...' inputs. I've solved this with strings.  
Hopefully this code has some hidden features in it that you may be interested in.

```{r generic loop - DRY but difficult}

random_number_generators <- c("runif", "rnorm", "rt,20", "rbeta,4,12")

# rng is an abbreviation for random number generator
for (generator_name in random_number_generators) {
  rng_command_with_args <- strsplit(generator_name, ",")[[1]]
  rng_command_name <- rng_command_with_args[1]
  rng_command <- get(rng_command_name)
  rng_args <- as.numeric(rng_command_with_args[-1])
  
  gen_dataset_arguments <- c(list(n=1000, m=200, func=rng_command ), as.list(rng_args))
  random_samples <- do.call(generate_dataset, gen_dataset_arguments)

  qqnorm(random_samples[[1]], main=paste("number generator distribution", rng_command_name))
  qqline(random_samples[[1]])
  
  mean_values <- calculate_mean_values(random_samples)

  qqnorm(mean_values, main=paste("distribution of means of", rng_command_name))
  qqline(mean_values)
}

```
